articles.body: Short answer: treat the original receipt as an audit record first, then choose multipart upload as the transport. Keep upload state in your database, keep the object immutable after completion, and make completion and abort explicit transitions. I run a one-person SaaS, so I measure infrastructure in revenue per hour. The useful question isn't “can this upload finish?” It's “can I explain exactly what happened to this receipt six months later?” Ship weekly. Outsource the undifferentiated transfer work, but keep the evidence boundary visible in code. Start with the evidence, not the upload call An AI-generated image, scanner capture, or phone photo can all become a receipt original. The bytes need one stable object key tied to a tenant and receipt identifier.

articles.title: Edge Rate Limits vs Application Limits: Closing a Login API Enumeration Gap
articles.excerpt: A login API can reject every incorrect password and still help an attacker prepare an account takeover campaign. If its responses reveal which email addresses exist, automation can turn a candidate li…
articles.body: A login API can reject every incorrect password and still help an attacker prepare an account takeover campaign. If its responses reveal which email addresses exist, automation can turn a candidate list into a verified target list. Those targets can then feed credential stuffing, password spraying, or targeted phishing. For security owners deciding how to block automated account enumeration on a login API, a useful comparison is A: rate limiting at the WAF edge versus B: limiting attempts inside the application . Each placement sees different evidence and controls a different part of the attack. Neither compensates for an endpoint that reliably discloses account existence.

articles.title: How to Block Automated Account Enumeration on a Login API
articles.excerpt: Account enumeration happens when a login API reveals whether an account exists. An attacker submits candidate email addresses or usernames, then compares error messages, status codes, response sizes,…
articles.body: Account enumeration happens when a login API reveals whether an account exists. An attacker submits candidate email addresses or usernames, then compares error messages, status codes, response sizes, or timing. The resulting list can support credential stuffing, targeted phishing, and account takeover. AI-assisted automation can help attackers generate candidate identities and adapt request patterns. For defenders, the practical concern is whether repeated requests reveal useful account information. This guide explains how to block automated account enumeration on a login API through application fixes, traffic controls, and verification. SafeLine is a self-hosted WAF that filters HTTP/S traffic as a reverse proxy.

articles.title: Build a Serverless Data Lake on AWS with S3, Glue and Athena
articles.excerpt: I wanted to answer questions like "which product category made the most money in March?" from a pile of CSV files, without standing up a database or a cluster. On AWS the answer is a small serverless…
articles.body: I wanted to answer questions like "which product category made the most money in March?" from a pile of CSV files, without standing up a database or a cluster. On AWS the answer is a small serverless data lake : the files stay in Amazon S3 , an AWS Glue crawler works out the schema, and Amazon Athena runs plain SQL against them. There's nothing to keep running, and I only pay for the data each query reads. In this post I'm building one with 150,000 synthetic e-commerce orders. Then I'm converting the data to Parquet and running the same query again. It read about 95% less data (12.6 MB down to 635 KB) and returned exactly the same answer.

articles.body: Full disclosure: I built a stitch-script tool on Capafy, so I'm biased. Everything below works with the source video's transcript, a notes app and about twenty minutes. You don't need the tool to use the method. TL;DR A stitch or duet borrows attention that already exists. The source video has done the hard part: people care about the topic. Your job is to add something worth watching after the handoff. Most response videos fail because they react instead of respond: "Wait, what? No. Okay so..." and then a ramble. Here's the fix: Transcribe the source and break down what it actually claims. Write your stance in one sentence. Choose the cut point in the source. Write three opening lines for the first second after the handoff. Script it shot by shot in two lengths.

articles.body: A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.
